title: Auxiliary modalities add no detectable discrimination or calibration over structured EHR for 30-day COPD readmission: evidence from a leakage-audited MIMIC-IV cohort
authors: M. Pozza, N. Navarin, S. Gabrielli
abstract: Background: Hospital readmission is a common and costly outcome in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Multimodal deep learning models combining structured electronic health record (EHR) data with physiological, imaging, and textual data have been proposed to improve its prediction, but whether such fusion outperforms EHR data alone, once temporal-leakage safeguards are applied, remains unclear. Methods: Using a stratified MIMIC-IV cohort of COPD patients enriched to about 50% readmission (natural prevalence 18.1%; n=1,279; 895/192/192 training/validation/test), we predicted 30-day, all-cause readmission from four frozen, pre-trained encoders (electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, clinical notes, structured EHR). We audited and corrected temporal leakage in the admission-linkage pipeline of each modality, then compared three fusion architectures (naive concatenation, scalar gated fusion, EHR-anchored residual fusion) against unimodal baselines and an EHR-alone reference, using bootstrap significance testing, a missingness stress test, and calibration analysis with and without post-hoc recalibration. Results: The audit corrected three previously undetected temporal-alignment issues, affecting 5-9% of patients for clinical notes, 29-43% for chest radiographs, and 53-58% for ECG. After correction, every modality except EHR showed near-chance discrimination alone (ROC-AUC 0.46-0.53), confirmed with a non-linear adapter probe. No fusion architecture significantly outperformed the EHR-alone baseline (ROC-AUC 0.63); removing auxiliary modalities improved rather than degraded fusion performance under stress testing. The raw Brier score was lower for all three fusion architectures than for EHR-alone (about 0.24 versus 0.32), but this reflected overconfidence of the EHR-alone probe (calibration slope 0.12); after logistic recalibration fitted on the validation set, Brier scores were indistinguishable (EHR-alone 0.239; fusion 0.240-0.244; all paired bootstrap 95% CIs included zero). Conclusions: Structured EHR data alone matched the discrimination and, after recalibration, the calibration of more complex multimodal fusion for 30-day COPD readmission prediction. These findings highlight the importance of rigorous temporal-leakage auditing in multimodal clinical prediction research and suggest that reformulating this task around temporal proximity to the outcome, rather than refining the fusion mechanism further, may be more productive for future work.

title: Insights on Designing the MINT (Micro-Interventions for Navigating Tension) Chatbot System for Stress Management: Collaborative Autoethnography
authors: M. Bolpagni, S.A. Piffer, M. Pozza, M. Maminimini, S. Gabrielli
abstract: Background: Digital microinterventions are increasingly used to support stress self-management in everyday life. While previous research has examined their feasibility, adherence, and preliminary effectiveness, much less is known about how these interventions are experienced over extended periods of real-world use.  Objective: This study used collaborative autoethnography (CAE) to examine the everyday experience of living with MINT (Micro-Interventions for Navigating Tension), a Telegram-based chatbot for stress management. Our goal was not to evaluate clinical outcomes but to understand how scheduled microinterventions fit into everyday life, when they were ignored, and when people relied on other ways of coping instead, and to identify implications for the design of future digital mental health tools.  Methods: We conducted a 4-week CAE involving 5 digital mental health researchers, who used the MINT chatbot as both participants and researchers. The experience was documented through multiple qualitative and quantitative sources, including reflective diaries, ecological momentary assessments (EMAs), workshop discussions, and wearable data, and analyzed collaboratively using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA).  Results: Six interconnected themes described how MINT was experienced in everyday life: (T1) the importance of timing and emotional receptivity, (T2) the need for reciprocity and relational continuity, (T3) the tendency to favor existing coping strategies over suggested exercises, (T4) the meaning of nonengagement during periods of high stress, (T5) the collapse of self-initiated use after reminders were removed, and (T6) how everyday experiences with consumer wearables and general-purpose large language models reshaped expectations of digital mental health systems.  Conclusions: Our findings show that CAE complements conventional evaluations of digital mental health interventions by revealing aspects of everyday use that are difficult to capture through feasibility studies, large-scale trials, or looking at usage data. Beyond the specific case of MINT, they suggest that future stress-management systems should better account for users’ receptivity, provide greater continuity across interactions, build on existing coping strategies, and help users move from externally prompted engagement to autonomous self-management.

title: Artificial Intelligence Methods and Digital Intervention Strategies for Predicting and Managing Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Exacerbations: An Umbrella Review
authors: M. Pozza, N. Navarin, V. Sakkalis, S. Gabrielli
abstract: Background: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a major global health burden in which acute exacerbations accelerate progression and increase hospitalizations. Emerging technologies, such as wearable biosensors, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital health tools, enable more proactive disease management. Objectives: This umbrella review synthesized evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses on (1) AI-driven prediction of COPD exacerbations using low-cost wearable biosignals, and (2) the effectiveness of digital health interventions on disease management, quality of life, and medication adherence. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (2015–2025) identified eligible reviews. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR-2, and study overlap was quantified with the Corrected Covered Area (CCA). A narrative synthesis was conducted across two research questions. Protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251164450). Results: Twenty-seven reviews met the inclusion criteria. AI models demonstrated promising internal predictive accuracy but lacked external validation and clinical integration. Digital health interventions, such as mHealth applications and telerehabilitation, showed small to moderate improvements in quality of life and physical function. Reported effects varied considerably (OR = 0.20–2.37; I2 = 0–94%), indicating substantial heterogeneity across studies. Evidence for improvements in medication adherence and exacerbation reduction was inconsistent, and most included reviews were rated “Low” or “Critically Low” in methodological quality, limiting the generalizability of findings. Conclusions: AI and digital tools show strong promise for proactive COPD management, particularly through wearable-derived biosignals, outperforming traditional static assessments. However, their clinical readiness remains limited due to small-scale studies, interpretability challenges, inconsistent outcome measures, and a lack of external validation. To support real-world translation and regulatory adoption, future research must prioritize large-scale, rigorous, and equitable studies with standardized methodologies and robust generalizability testing.

title: A systematic review of cross-patient approaches for EEG epileptic seizure prediction
authors: S. Shafiezadeh, G.M. Duma, M. Pozza, A. Testolin
abstract: Objective: Seizure prediction could greatly improve the quality of life of people suffering from epilepsy. Modern prediction systems leverage artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to automatically analyze neurophysiological data, most commonly the electroencephalogram (EEG), in order to anticipate upcoming epileptic events. However, the performance of these systems is normally assessed using randomized splitting methods, which can suffer from data leakage and thus result in an optimistic evaluation. In this review, we systematically surveyed the available scientific literature looking for research approaches that adopted more stringent assessment methods based on patient-independent testing. Approach: We queried three scientific databases (PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science), focusing on AI techniques based on non-invasive EEG recorded from human subjects. We first summarize a standardized signal processing pipeline that could be deployed for the development and testing of cross-patient seizure prediction systems. We then analyze the research work that meets our selection criteria. Main results: 21 articles adopted patient-independent validation methods, constituting only 4% of the published work in the entire field of epileptic seizure prediction. Among eligible articles, the most common approach to deal with cross-patient scenarios was based on source domain adaptation techniques, which allow to fine-tune the predictive model on a limited set of data recorded from a set of independent target patients. Significance: Overall, our review indicates that epileptic seizure prediction remains an extremely challenging problem and significant research efforts are still needed to develop automated systems that can be deployed in realistic clinical settings. Our review protocol is based on the preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis protocols 2020 guidelines for conducting systematic reviews, considering NHLBI and ROBIS tools to mitigate the risk of bias, and it was pre-registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD4202452317).

title: A Comparison of Recurrent and Convolutional Deep Learning Architectures for EEG Seizure Forecasting
authors: S. Shafiezadeh, M. Pozza, A. Testolin
abstract: Many research efforts are being spent to discover predictive markers of seizures, which would allow to build forecasting systems that could mitigate the risk of injuries and clinical complications in epileptic patients. Although electroencephalography (EEG) is the most widely used tool to monitor abnormal brain electrical activity, no commercial devices can reliably anticipate seizures from EEG signal analysis at present. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence, particularly deep learning algorithms, show promise in enhancing EEG classifier forecasting accuracy by automatically extracting relevant spatio-temporal features from EEG recordings. In this study, we systematically compare the predictive accuracy of two leading deep learning architectures: recurrent models based on Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). To this aim, we consider a data set of long-term, continuous multi-channel EEG recordings collected from 29 epileptic patients, and we evaluate the performance of both architectures in predicting seizure occurrences up to 30 minutes in advance.
venue: Proceedings of the 17th International Joint Conference on Biomedical Engineering Systems and Technologies (BIOSTEC 2024)
